lesson.title: Leftover Parts: Vestigial Structures
lesson.summary: Vestigial structures are reduced, often functionally minor remnants of structures that were fully functional in an ancestral species, retained in modified or shrunken form because there has not been strong enough selective pressure to eliminate them entirely.
lesson.body:
Homologous structures do not always stay fully functional on every branch of the family tree. Sometimes a structure that was essential to an ancestor becomes reduced, simplified, or largely nonfunctional in a descendant lineage, usually because that lineage's way of life stopped requiring it. Biologists call what is left behind a vestigial structure: a reduced remnant of an ancestral structure, homologous to the fully developed version still found in related species, but no longer serving its original purpose.

This connects directly to homology, because a vestigial structure is a homologous structure by definition. It is still built from the same underlying architecture inherited from a common ancestor, just scaled down or simplified because natural selection stopped maintaining its original form. A useful example is the pelvis and tiny leg bones found buried in the body wall of modern whales, remnants of the fully functional hind limbs their four legged, land dwelling ancestors used to walk, recalling the whale fossil sequence from the fossil record chapter. Those bones no longer connect to functional legs and play no role in swimming, but their presence, in the same relative position and built from recognizably the same bone types as a land mammal's pelvis and hind limb, only makes sense as an inherited, reduced remnant of a structure their ancestors actually used.

This is also where natural selection explains something that might otherwise seem puzzling: if a structure is no longer useful, why has it not simply disappeared? The answer is that natural selection does not eliminate a structure just because it is unused. It eliminates or reduces a structure only when keeping it imposes enough of a cost to reduce an organism's survival or reproduction relative to individuals with a smaller or absent version. A small, buried pelvic bone in a whale costs very little in terms of energy or interference with swimming, so there has been comparatively weak selective pressure to shrink or remove it further, and it has persisted, reduced but present, across many generations. Where a structure does impose a real cost, selection can reduce it much further. Where the cost is negligible, a reduced vestige can persist essentially indefinitely.

Humans carry several vestigial structures of our own. The coccyx, at the base of the human spine, is a reduced remnant of the tail present in other primates and, further back, in our non-primate ancestors. Arrector pili, tiny muscles attached to each hair follicle, still contract in response to cold or fear, producing goosebumps, a reflex that in a fur covered ancestor would fluff the coat for insulation or to look larger to a threat, but that does essentially nothing useful on the comparatively hairless skin of a modern human. The human appendix, a narrow pouch attached to the large intestine, is a reduced remnant of a much larger ancestral cecum, a structure still large and functional in many modern plant eating mammals, where it houses bacteria that help digest tough, cellulose rich plant material. It is worth noting that some structures once labeled purely vestigial turn out, on closer study, to retain a minor secondary function. There is ongoing research into a possible minor immune role for the human appendix, for instance, but that does not undo its status as a reduced homolog of a structure that did much more in the ancestral condition. Being vestigial is about reduction relative to an ancestral structure's original function, not about being completely and permanently useless in every respect.
